explanations.answer: He didn't call them to fight Midian
explanations.explanation: Ephraim's men ask, “Why did you fail to call us when you went to fight against Midian?” (Judges 8:1). That's the whole complaint, right there in the text. They felt left off the list, and they came to say so out loud. I spent years in the back of a junk drawer, so I know a little about being left out.

explanations.answer: He kept the plunder for himself
explanations.explanation: The text never says anything about plunder in this complaint. What Ephraim asks is why Gideon failed to call them when he went to fight Midian (Judges 8:1). It's easy to assume a fight over loot, but this one is about being left out of the battle. Stick with what the verse says, friend.

explanations.answer: He put Manasseh in charge of them
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says Gideon put Manasseh over Ephraim. The men of Ephraim ask why he failed to call them when he went to fight Midian (Judges 8:1). Their anger is about being left out of the fight. Nobody in this verse is arguing about who's the boss.

The text says it plainly: “And they contended with him violently.” (Judges 8:1). This wasn't a polite note in the suggestion box. These men came in hot, and Gideon is standing right there in the middle of it.
The text says the men of Ephraim “contended with him violently.” (Judges 8:1). So this was no calm chat over cookies. They came to Gideon angry and they let him have it.

explanations.answer: Oreb and Zeeb the princes of Midian
explanations.explanation: Gideon says, “God has delivered Oreb and Zeeb, the two princes of Midian, into your hand.” (Judges 8:3). Notice who he says did the delivering: God. Then he asks what he was able to do compared to them. That's a man handing out the credit instead of keeping it.

explanations.answer: Zebah and Zalmunna the kings of Midian
explanations.explanation: Zebah and Zalmunna are the kings of Midian, and Gideon is still chasing them in this passage (Judges 8:5). The ones God delivered into Ephraim's hand were two princes, Oreb and Zeeb (Judges 8:3). Princes and kings are easy to mix up, so no shame in a stumble here.

explanations.answer: The whole camp of the Midianites
explanations.explanation: Gideon doesn't talk about a whole camp here. He names two men: “Oreb and Zeeb, the two princes of Midian.” (Judges 8:3). Those are the ones he says God delivered into Ephraim's hand.
The text says, “When he had said this, their anger against him subsided.” (Judges 8:3). Gideon's answer took the fire out of the room. I've seen a good word do what a rolling pin never could.
The text goes the other way. After Gideon speaks, their anger against him subsided (Judges 8:3). He walked in facing a storm and the storm settled down.
The text doesn't say the anger came back. It says that after Gideon spoke, their anger against him subsided (Judges 8:3). That's the end of the argument in this passage.
Gideon says, “Please give my troops some bread…” (Judges 8:5). That's the whole ask. No fancy feast, just bread for tired men.

Gideon says his troops need bread “for they are exhausted” (Judges 8:5). The text says the same thing earlier, that they crossed the Jordan exhausted yet still in pursuit (Judges 8:4). I know that tired. It's the tired where even a crumb looks like a good deal.
Gideon doesn't ask for swords. He asks for bread (Judges 8:5). His men were tired and hungry, and a sword doesn't fix either one.
The text doesn't say his troops were wounded. It says they were exhausted (Judges 8:5). Same long road, different problem.
No horns come up in this request. Gideon asks for bread (Judges 8:5). He wanted something to put in tired men, not something to blow.

The leaders of Succoth don't hand over anything. They ask, “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession, that we should give bread to your army?” (Judges 8:6). That's a question wearing a refusal. Tired men asked for bread and got a puzzle.

The leaders of Succoth answer with a question: “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession, that we should give bread to your army?” (Judges 8:6). So the answer is no bread, not yet. They weren't happy to feed anybody.

explanations.answer: When the LORD hands him the two kings
explanations.explanation: Gideon says, “…when the LORD has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand…” (Judges 8:7). That's his timeline. He's saying that once the two kings are in his hand, he'll come back to Succoth. Notice he says the LORD is the one who delivers.

explanations.answer: When the men of Ephraim catch up
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't tie Gideon's warning to Ephraim at all. He says, “…when the LORD has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand…” (Judges 8:7). The timer is the two kings.

explanations.answer: When the barley harvest is over
explanations.explanation: No harvest comes up in his warning. Gideon says, “…when the LORD has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand…” (Judges 8:7). His clock runs on the capture of the two kings.

explanations.answer: They refuse him just like Succoth
explanations.explanation: The text says, “the men of Penuel gave the same response as the men of Succoth.” (Judges 8:8). Two towns asked, two towns turned him down. Gideon went looking for a kind word and came up empty twice.

explanations.answer: They give his men bread and water
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite. The men of Penuel “gave the same response as the men of Succoth.” (Judges 8:8). And Succoth had just turned him down, so no bread came from Penuel either.

explanations.answer: They send men to join the chase
explanations.explanation: Penuel doesn't send anybody. They gave the same response as the men of Succoth (Judges 8:8), and Succoth had refused him. His three hundred stayed three hundred.
Gideon tells the men of Penuel, “When I return in triumph, I will tear down this tower!” (Judges 8:9). He points at one particular tower. And he says he'll do it when he comes back in triumph.
A wall isn't what Gideon names. He says, “When I return in triumph, I will tear down this tower!” (Judges 8:9). Keep your eyes on the tower, friend, because it comes back later in this passage.
Gideon doesn't mention a gate. His words are, “When I return in triumph, I will tear down this tower!” (Judges 8:9). The tower is what he has his eye on.

The text says, “A hundred and twenty thousand swordsmen had already fallen.” (Judges 8:10). Then it says the fifteen thousand left were all that remained of the armies of the people of the east. That's a LOT of swords already gone before Gideon goes after the last of them.
That number is double what the text gives. It says a hundred and twenty thousand swordsmen had already fallen (Judges 8:10). The fifteen thousand at Karkor were all that were left of those armies.
The text gives a different number. It says “A hundred and twenty thousand swordsmen had already fallen.” (Judges 8:10). It's a big number either way, so I won't blame a baker for slipping.
The text says Gideon “attacked their army, taking them by surprise.” (Judges 8:11). He came by the caravan route, east of Nobah and Jogbehah. Fifteen thousand men didn't see him coming.
The text says Gideon attacked their army, “taking them by surprise.” (Judges 8:11). He went up by way of the caravan route east of Nobah and Jogbehah. So the army at Karkor was caught off guard.

The text says, “When Zebah and Zalmunna fled, Gideon pursued and captured these two kings of Midian…” (Judges 8:12). They ran and he ran after them. The chase that started back at the Jordan ends right here.
They run, but they don't get away. The text says Gideon pursued and captured the two kings of Midian (Judges 8:12). So the desert didn't save them.
This verse doesn't mention Ephraim at all. It says Gideon pursued and captured the two kings of Midian (Judges 8:12). Capturing is what happens here.

The text says the young man “wrote down for him the names of the seventy-seven leaders and elders of Succoth.” (Judges 8:14). So Gideon walks away with a list. Seventy-seven names is a long list for one captured young man to write.
The young man doesn't write down homes. He writes down the names of the seventy-seven leaders and elders of Succoth (Judges 8:14). It's a list of people, not places.
The text says nothing about debts. The young man wrote down the names of Succoth's seventy-seven leaders and elders (Judges 8:14). Names were the whole list.
Gideon says, “Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me…” (Judges 8:15). These are the two kings Succoth said weren't in his hand yet. Now they stand right in front of the town.

Oreb and Zeeb are the two princes of Midian from the Ephraim moment (Judges 8:3). Succoth's question was about Zebah and Zalmunna, and those are the ones Gideon shows them (Judges 8:15). Two sets of Midian names in one chapter, I'll give you that.

Joash is Gideon's father, named in this passage as the father of “Gideon son of Joash” (Judges 8:13). But he isn't who Gideon shows Succoth. He shows them Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings they had taunted him about (Judges 8:15).

The text says the opposite. “He also pulled down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.” (Judges 8:17). The tower he warned about in verse 9 comes down. I think this part is heavy, so we'll handle it with care.

The text says, “He also pulled down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.” (Judges 8:17). That's the tower Gideon had promised to tear down (Judges 8:9). This is a heavy part of the passage, and I won't make light of it.
The kings answer, “Men like you…each one resembling the son of a king.” (Judges 8:18). They say the men they killed looked like Gideon himself. It's a heavy answer for Gideon to hear.
Shepherds aren't what the kings say. Their answer is, “Men like you,” and they add, “each one resembling the son of a king.” (Judges 8:18). They compared the men to Gideon.
The kings don't say soldiers. They say, “Men like you,” and then, “each one resembling the son of a king.” (Judges 8:18). They pointed straight at Gideon.

Gideon says, “They were my brothers…the sons of my mother!” (Judges 8:19). So the question about Tabor wasn't random. This is family, and I think it hurts. He adds that if they had let them live, he would not kill them.
Gideon doesn't say servants. He says, “They were my brothers…the sons of my mother!” (Judges 8:19). That's why the kings' answer lands so hard.
Cousins aren't in the text. Gideon says, “They were my brothers…the sons of my mother!” (Judges 8:19). Brothers from the same mother is as close as it gets.

The text says the opposite. Gideon tells Jether to get up and kill the kings, “But the young man did not draw his sword; he was fearful because he was still a youth.” (Judges 8:20). Jether is Gideon's firstborn. The sword stayed in its sheath.

The text says, “But the young man did not draw his sword; he was fearful because he was still a youth.” (Judges 8:20). Jether, Gideon's firstborn, stood there with his sword put away. A young man, a hard order, and a heavy moment.

The text says Gideon “took the crescent ornaments from the necks of their camels.” (Judges 8:21). The kings' camels were wearing them. It's a small detail, and the text puts it right at the end of the scene.
Bells aren't in this verse. The text says Gideon took “the crescent ornaments from the necks of their camels.” (Judges 8:21). I know a bell or two, and these weren't them.
The text doesn't say clasps. Gideon took “the crescent ornaments from the necks of their camels.” (Judges 8:21). Crescents are the word you want.
